analysis.one_liner: Cancels two years of automatic spending cuts and pays for it by closing offshore tax loopholes.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in December 2013, referred to three House committees, and never received a hearing, vote, or further action before the Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have canceled the automatic across-the-board federal spending cuts (the "sequester") for 2014 and 2015, which trimmed everything from medical research to defense, and would have made up the money by shutting down ways that corporations and wealthy individuals move profits into offshore tax havens. It would have taxed offshore profit-shifting more aggressively, forced public companies to report country-by-country where they earn money and pay taxes, and given the Treasury new power against foreign banks that help Americans hide money. It was introduced by Rep. Rosa DeLauro in December 2013 and was never taken up by any of the three committees it was sent to; it died when the Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, ordinary taxpayers would have benefited twice: the sequester cuts to programs like medical research, education, and public safety would have been repealed (the bill's findings cite CBO estimates that repealing the 2014 sequester alone would add 800,000 jobs and 0.6 percent to GDP), and the cost would have fallen on multinational corporations and offshore financial institutions rather than on the deficit. Domestic businesses that pay taxes without havens would also have faced fairer competition from rivals that shift profits abroad.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and recipients of federal programs

how_it_helps.text: Title I repeals the across-the-board sequestration cuts for fiscal 2014 and 2015 and raises the fiscal 2016 spending caps, ending cuts to programs the bill's findings list as medical research, education, and public safety.

The bill's findings cite Congressional Budget Office analysis that repealing the 2014 sequester would increase real GDP by 0.6 percent and employment by 800,000 jobs, and note that discretionary spending would otherwise fall $123 billion (11 percent) below its 2010 level.

The spending is offset by taxing offshore profit-shifting: deductions tied to deferred foreign income are limited, foreign corporations managed from the United States are taxed as domestic, 'check-the-box' rules that let companies erase foreign subsidiaries are repealed for certain entities, and swap payments sent offshore are taxed as U.S. income.

Enforcement provisions let Treasury restrict banks and jurisdictions that impede U.S. tax enforcement, create rebuttable presumptions that money in non-compliant offshore institutions belongs to the U.S. person behind it, require public country-by-country reporting of profits and taxes, and extend anti-money-laundering rules to investment advisers and company formation agents.

analysis.who_pays: Multinational corporations using offshore profit-shifting (the bill's findings estimate $150 billion a year in lost federal revenue from such schemes), financial institutions and advisers in offshore secrecy jurisdictions facing new reporting and anti-money-laundering rules, and publicly traded companies that would have to disclose country-by-country profits and taxes.

drawbacks.text: The bill's reporting rules, presumptions of control over offshore entities, and new anti-money-laundering duties would impose substantial compliance costs on banks, investment advisers, company formation agents, and multinationals, and broad presumptions tied to any institution that does not fully comply with FATCA reporting could ensnare ordinary Americans with legitimate offshore accounts unless regulators carve out exceptions.

The introduced text's fiscal-year 2016 spending-cap increases are written as roughly $22,992,000,000,000 for security and $15,652,000,000,000 for nonsecurity — figures in the trillions that appear to be drafting errors for billions — and no committee ever reviewed or corrected the bill.

The CBO job and growth figures cited in the findings (800,000 jobs, 0.6 percent GDP) come from the bill's own statements about sequestration repeal, not from a scored estimate of the full bill, and the bill never received a hearing where the revenue offsets could be examined.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is honest on its face: restore roughly $123 billion of scheduled spending cuts and, per the CBO figures cited in the bill's own findings, add about 800,000 jobs, while paying for it by taxing offshore profits and cracking down on havens rather than adding to the deficit. The main costs are compliance complexity for banks and multinationals and some risk that broad presumptions could sweep in ordinary people with legitimate offshore accounts. The deeper problem is that the bill was never tested: no hearing, no mark-up, no committee report, and the fiscal-year 2016 cap figures in the introduced text are written in trillions of dollars rather than billions, a drafting error that a single committee review would have caught. As introduced, it was a statement of priorities rather than ready-to-enact law.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three committees on the day it was introduced, none of which ever took it up, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro, joined by Rep. Lloyd Doggett, introduced the bill on December 5, 2013.
The same day, the Speaker referred it to the Ways and Means, Financial Services, and Budget Committees; the action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action ever followed.
The 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015, and the bill expired without a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Multinational corporations and the offshore banks, advisers, and formation agents that profit from tax-haven structures were better off, since no enforcement or disclosure regime advanced; the automatic spending cuts also remained in place.

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican signed on, but with no hearing or roll-call vote the record never shows where the broader chambers stood.

industries.industry: Multinational corporations using offshore tax havens
industries.note: Title IV curtails the main tools for shifting profits offshore: deductions tied to deferred foreign income, intangible-property transfers, 'check-the-box' entity classification, and loans from foreign subsidiaries to U.S. parents. The bill's findings estimate about $150 billion a year in lost federal revenue from such schemes and note 83 of the top 100 public companies had haven subsidiaries.

industries.industry: Offshore banks and secrecy-jurisdiction financial institutions
industries.note: Treasury could restrict correspondent accounts and card use for institutions that impede U.S. tax enforcement, and tax courts could presume money in non-FATCA-compliant institutions belongs to the U.S. person behind it. Their business model of opaque accounts for foreigners is directly targeted.

industries.industry: Investment advisers and company formation agents
industries.note: Both would become subject to Bank Secrecy Act anti-money-laundering programs, suspicious-activity reporting, and customer identification rules, closing the channel through which anonymous shell entities are created.

New SEC rules would require annual country-by-country disclosure of employees, revenues, and taxes paid to every government, with civil penalties up to $10 million per violation for knowingly concealing offshore holdings. The point is to let investors and the public see where profits sit versus where work is done.

industries.industry: Defense contractors and providers of federally funded domestic programs
industries.note: Repealing the 2014–2015 sequester restores the automatic cuts to both defense and nondefense spending, protecting procurement, medical research, education, and public safety budgets that the cuts would have reduced.
